newsitem.title: LEBANON: Police clash with Beirut demonstrators.
newsitem.headline: Police clash with Beirut demonstrators.

text.p: Protests against the Lebanese government's plans to reorganise the media erupted in street clashes on Wednesday as police blocked demonstrators trying to march on the office of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.

Lines of police armed with automatic rifles blocked the way as hundreds of demonstrators, some with banners proclaiming "Repression is killing Lebanon", tried to march on Hariri's office to stage a sit-in outside the building.

The demonstrators were demanding cancellation of a new law under which the government plans to close most of Lebanon's many private radio and television stations and licence only a handful of stations owned by powerful establishment figures.

The measure will put 3,000 media workers out of work. Newspapers and opposition politicians say it is an attempt to muzzle opposition radio and television stations and carve up lucrative media franchises among government supporters.

Lebanon's Catholic bishops are outraged that their religious television and two radios are to close. They have rejected a government proposal for the official media to broadcast religious programmes instead, saying this could lead to censorship of Christian self-expression.

Fist fights broke out 150 metres (yards) from Hariri's office as the demonstrators, led by labour confederation chief Elias Abu Rizk, tried to push through a cordon of riot police in helmets and carrying plastic shields, batons and rifles.
Demonstrators shouting "Down with Hariri, down with Hariri," hit the police with sticks from their banners and scuffles continued for two or three minutes before the crowd retreated.
A second brief clash took place when another group of police blocked the demonstrators' retreat and clubbed them with rifle butts before the crowd retreated again and dispersed.
Abu Rizk, an outspoken foe of Hariri, was among those clubbed on the legs and chest in the second clash.
Under the new law organising the audiovisual media, the government has licenced four private television stations and 11 radios. Dozens of televisions and more than 100 radios will have to close.
No opposition radio or television station is among those which have received licences.

Opponents of the law are particularly angry that the government has granted three of the four television licences to Hariri, parliament Speaker Nabih Berri and Interior Minister Michel al-Murr. Berri's televison has not yet been formed, while well-known stations which have broadcast for years are to close.
Some of Lebanon's best-known and most professional private radio stations will also to be shut down under the law, which is due to take effect in November.
